blocks.text: 1. Learning Curves

blocks.alt: An epoch and a loss value together form a learning curve

blocks.text: Hyperparameters, the previous topic, surveyed the many tunable settings that shape training. Learning Curves are the genuinely essential tool for visualizing how training actually plays out under whatever hyperparameters get chosen.
A learning curve plots loss, or another metric, against epochs or iterations, both already covered in earlier topics, a genuinely direct, visual window into training explored throughout this topic.
2. What Actually Gets Plotted

blocks.alt: Train loss and validation loss both get plotted over epochs

blocks.text: This connects back to loss, already covered throughout the Loss Functions module. Training loss and validation loss, plotted together on the same chart, are the genuinely most common learning curve of all.
These form two genuinely separate lines, tracked across epochs, already covered, letting a single glance reveal how each one evolves over the entire course of training.

blocks.text: 3. What A Genuinely Healthy Curve Looks Like

blocks.alt: Both lines fall together and stay close together

blocks.text: A genuinely healthy learning curve shows both training loss and validation loss decreasing together, then genuinely leveling off as training approaches a good, stable solution.
This is a strong, direct visual signal that training is genuinely working well, with the network learning genuinely useful patterns that transfer from training data to validation data alike.
4. Recognizing Underfitting On The Curve

blocks.alt: Both lines staying high and flat signals underfitting

blocks.text: This connects back to underfitting, already covered in its own topic. On a learning curve, underfitting shows up as both training loss and validation loss staying genuinely high, neither improving much over time.
This is a direct, visual confirmation of underfitting, already covered, since the network has not managed to learn even the training data well, let alone generalize to new data.
5. Recognizing Overfitting On The Curve

blocks.alt: Train falling while validation rises signals overfitting

blocks.text: This connects back to overfitting, already covered in its own topic. On a learning curve, overfitting shows up as training loss continuing to decrease while validation loss genuinely starts rising instead.
This is a direct, visual confirmation of overfitting, already covered, since the network keeps improving on training data while genuinely losing its ability to generalize to new, unseen data.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: A rising validation loss combined with a still-falling training loss, already covered in this topic, is one of the single clearest, most actionable warning signs available during training.

blocks.text: 6. Interpreting The Gap Between The Two Lines

blocks.alt: A small gap signals good generalization while a large gap signals overfitting

blocks.text: This connects back to the Bias-Variance Tradeoff, already covered in its own topic. The genuine gap between training loss and validation loss acts as a direct, visual proxy for variance, already covered there.

A genuinely large, growing gap signals genuinely high variance, while a genuinely small, stable gap signals genuinely low variance, giving a concrete, visual way to reason about that earlier topic's own abstract concept.
7. The Connection To Early Stopping

This connects back to Early Stopping, already covered in the Regularization Techniques module. The exact point where validation loss stops improving is genuinely visible directly on the curve, already covered throughout this topic.

This is a genuinely direct, visual justification for that technique's own stopping rule, turning what might otherwise seem like an arbitrary cutoff into a genuinely clear, observable moment on the chart itself.
8. Learning Curves Beyond Just Loss

blocks.alt: Learning curves cover both a loss curve and an accuracy curve

blocks.text: A genuinely important generalization follows. This connects forward to Evaluation Metrics, covered later in this course. Learning curves are not limited to loss alone; accuracy or other metrics can be plotted the same way.

Any metric tracked across epochs or iterations, already covered, can form its own learning curve, giving a genuinely flexible tool that extends well beyond just the loss values already covered throughout most of this topic.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When To Genuinely Rely On Learning Curves
Diagnosing whether a model is underfitting or overfitting, both already covered, is a direct case where learning curves, already covered in this topic, give a genuinely direct, visual answer.

Deciding when to stop training, or whether current hyperparameters, already covered, are genuinely working, is another genuine case where watching the curves in real time offers genuinely immediate, actionable feedback.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates generating and interpreting a genuinely simple learning curve, simulating both a healthy pattern and an overfitting pattern already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

epochs = np.arange(1, 21)

# Simulating a genuinely healthy learning curve, already covered in this topic
healthy_train_loss = 2.0 * np.exp(-0.2 * epochs) + 0.1
healthy_val_loss = 2.0 * np.exp(-0.18 * epochs) + 0.15

# Simulating an overfitting learning curve, already covered in this topic
overfit_train_loss = 2.0 * np.exp(-0.3 * epochs) + 0.05
overfit_val_loss = 2.0 * np.exp(-0.2 * epochs) + 0.15 + 0.02 * np.maximum(0, epochs - 10)

print("Epoch | Healthy train | Healthy val | Overfit train | Overfit val")
for i in [0, 4, 9, 14, 19]:
    print(f"{epochs[i]:5d} | {healthy_train_loss[i]:13.3f} | {healthy_val_loss[i]:11.3f} | {overfit_train_loss[i]:14.3f} | {overfit_val_loss[i]:11.3f}")

print("\nNotice the overfit validation loss starts rising after epoch 10, already covered as recognizing overfitting on the curve in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the overfitting pattern's validation loss column turning upward partway through training, exactly the warning sign already covered in this topic as the clearest indicator of overfitting.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A learning curve plots loss, or another metric, against epochs or iterations.
Training loss and validation loss, plotted together, form the most common learning curve.
A healthy curve shows both lines decreasing together, then leveling off.
Both lines staying high indicates underfitting.
Training loss falling while validation loss rises indicates overfitting.
The gap between the two lines acts as a visual proxy for variance.
The point where validation loss stops improving visually justifies Early Stopping.
Learning curves extend beyond loss to any tracked metric, including accuracy.
